Compute cosine similarity between embeddings

Source: R/similarity.R
topic_similarity.Rd

topic_similarity() computes the cosine similarity between every row of x and every row of y, or between all pairs of rows of x when y is omitted. In a sentence-embedding space, the closeness of two texts in meaning is measured by the cosine of the angle between their embeddings: 1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated directions, and negative values for opposed ones; cosine similarity ignores vector length, so it compares texts of different lengths on an equal footing.

Rows are scaled to unit length first, so embeddings need not be normalized. The result is a matrix, or with tidy = TRUE a long data frame with one row per pair. With top, the data frame keeps only the nearest neighbors of each row of x: its top most similar rows of y, most similar first, where a row is not its own neighbor when y is omitted.

Any embeddings can be compared: texts from encode(), the bundled feedback_embeddings, or rows of another embedding matrix with the same number of columns. To assign texts to fitted topics use predict(); to relate the topics of a model to one another use topic_hierarchy().

Usage

topic_similarity(x, y = NULL, tidy = FALSE, top = NULL)

Arguments

x

Numeric embedding matrix, or a numeric vector (one embedding).

y

Numeric embedding matrix or vector, or NULL (default) to compare the rows of x with each other.

tidy

FALSE (default) for a matrix; TRUE for a data frame.

top

NULL (default) for every pair, or a whole number: with tidy = TRUE, the top most similar rows of y for each row of x.

Value

With tidy = FALSE, a numeric matrix of similarities in [-1, 1] with one row per row of x and one column per row of y (or of x); a vector counts as one row. With tidy = TRUE, a base data frame with one row per pair and columns from (row of x), to (row of y), and similarity; from and to are row names when the matrices have them, else row numbers. With top, at most top rows per row of x, ordered by from and decreasing similarity (ties by position in y), with a rank column (1 for the most similar).

Conditions

sbert_dimension_mismatch when x and y have different numbers of columns; sbert_bad_input when a row is zero, or when top is given without tidy = TRUE.

See also

encode() for embeddings; predict() to assign texts to topics; topic_hierarchy() for similarity between topics.

Examples

# Three feedback messages compared with each other.
topic_similarity(head(feedback_embeddings, 3))
#>            [,1]       [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,] 1.00000000 0.36132672 0.09539736
#> [2,] 0.36132672 1.00000000 0.09345878
#> [3,] 0.09539736 0.09345878 1.00000000
topic_similarity(head(feedback_embeddings, 3), tidy = TRUE)
#>   from to similarity
#> 1    1  1 1.00000000
#> 2    2  1 0.36132672
#> 3    3  1 0.09539736
#> 4    1  2 0.36132672
#> 5    2  2 1.00000000
#> 6    3  2 0.09345878
#> 7    1  3 0.09539736
#> 8    2  3 0.09345878
#> 9    3  3 1.00000000

# The three nearest neighbors of each of the 600 messages.
neighbors <- topic_similarity(feedback_embeddings, tidy = TRUE, top = 3)
head(neighbors)
#>   from  to similarity rank
#> 1    1   4  0.4894304    1
#> 2    1 566  0.4232803    2
#> 3    1 227  0.3940784    3
#> 4    2 475  0.8977640    1
#> 5    2  10  0.8975812    2
#> 6    2   9  0.8695729    3

# Toy vectors: rows of x against one vector y.
x <- rbind(c(1, 0), c(0, 1), c(1, 1))
topic_similarity(x, c(1, 1))
#>           [,1]
#> [1,] 0.7071068
#> [2,] 0.7071068
#> [3,] 1.0000000
